claims.text: Removing Co from FeNiCrMn increases the alloy's stacking-fault energy.
The increased stacking-fault energy shifts the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation slip to mechanical twinning.
A slip-to-twinning transition causes an anomalous change in strain-hardening behavior.
A slip-to-twinning transition changes yield strength relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has an as-solidified, fine-grained microstructure.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Stacking-fault energy affects the balance between dislocation glide and mechanical twinning.
Deformation-induced twin boundaries modulate dislocation mobility.
Twin boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Twinning-induced barriers enhance strain hardening in the Co-free alloy.
Twinning-induced barriers modify the Co-free alloy's yield behavior.
Within the proposed regime, Co-free FeNiCrMn will develop a higher deformation-twin density than CoCrFeMnNi.
Within the proposed regime, Co-free FeNiCrMn will show a corresponding shift in strain-hardening rate relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Outside the critical regime, deformation in the two alloys will converge toward dislocation-dominated behavior.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is predominantly dislocation-slip controlled and has lower twin density under identical conditions.

The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to approximately 600 degrees Celsius and at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 per second, provided precipitation and phase transformation are absent.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis associates increased stacking-fault energy with enhanced twinning, whereas the cited evidence associates negative stacking-fault energy with high twinning propensity and a comparatively high value of 49.7 mJ/m2 with dislocation-glide-controlled deformation.
